title: A (Political) Battle of the Sexes: Gender Polarization on Gender‐Related Attitudes Across 14 Societies
content:
An examination of gender-related attitudes across 14 countries showed that endorsement of old-fashioned forms of sexism (men's superiority and traditional gender roles) is inversely related to country-level gender equality for women and men, whereas modern sexism (denial of gender discrimination and belief that men are disadvantaged) was inversely related to gender equality among women, but not men. Thus, modern forms of sexism in egalitarian societies showed the largest gender gaps.


ABSTRACT

Although it is well-established that women typically endorse more progressive gender-related attitudes compared to men, key questions remain about the magnitude of this gender difference and whether it systematically varies in relation to levels of gender inequality across societies. In the current research, we aim to address these questions by examining endorsement of traditional (overt) and modern (indirect) forms of sexism across 14 countries, including those with relatively low levels of gender equality (e.g., Saudi Arabia, India, and Egypt) and those with relatively high equality (e.g., Sweden, the United Kingdom, and the United States). Results show that endorsement of old-fashioned sexism is inversely related to country-level gender equality for women and men, whereas modern sexism endorsement is inversely related to gender equality for women, but not men. Thus, gender polarization is largest on modern sexist attitudes in relatively high gender-equal countries, and this is because in such contexts modern forms of sexism are especially likely to be rejected by women.
